title: I built 20 reusable skills to make AI coding agents better at actual game development (3D, animation, VFX, debugging)
author: Fine-Reflection-7530
selftext:
I've been experimenting with AI-assisted game development, and one thing that kept bothering me was how easily AI agents could declare a task finished when the result was still visibly wrong or the feature hadn't actually been tested.

So I started building **ForgeSkills**, an open-source collection of 20 reusable skills for AI coding agents focused on the actual game development workflow, not just generating code.

The idea is to give agents concrete procedures to follow instead of relying on vague instructions like "make it look better" or "fix the animation."

Some of what's included:

* **Reference-to-3D reconstruction:** Rebuilding assets from reference images and tracking visual differences instead of making something vaguely similar.
* **Blender automation and procedural modeling:** Creating and iterating on game-ready assets.
* **Animation and locomotion:** Addressing things like foot sliding, awkward transitions, and movement that feels wrong.
* **VFX and game feel:** Impact effects, hit stop, camera response, and coordinated feedback.
* **Gameplay engineering:** Implementing game systems with explicit requirements and validation.
* **Debugging and verification:** Reproducing issues, isolating causes, testing fixes, and checking that the result actually works.

The core workflow is:

`Measure → Build → Render → Compare → Fix → Repeat`

There are also supporting Python tools for parts of the workflow that can be measured or checked automatically.

The repository currently includes Godot and Unity pipeline skills, alongside Blender and engine-independent workflows. It's designed to work with AI coding agents that support the standard [`SKILL.md`](http://SKILL.md) format.

**GitHub:** [https://github.com/sekaikx/ForgeSkills](https://github.com/sekaikx/ForgeSkills)

It's open source under Apache-2.0.

This is still a work in progress, and I'd appreciate feedback from people who use AI agents to build actual games. I'm particularly interested in what breaks in practice, which workflows are missing, and how to make the skills more reliable with weaker models.

If you try any of them, I'd love to hear what worked and what didn't.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
I was gonna say, Ive been experimenting with the blender MCP and all of this is just... what it already does if I tell it to.

This seems like another YouTube guru that heard "skills=good" and slapped something together like it's a magic bullet when all it does is bloat your prompt and introduce noise.  The MCP server already ships with a set of skills made by the people who made the MCP.

replies.author: Fine-Reflection-7530
replies.body:
yeah fair, Blender MCP already does a lot of this. i'm not saying my skills are some magic fix lol.

the stuff i was trying to capture was problems people actually ran into, like:

* AI generated 16 wall pieces for a house and only 4 were usable, with inconsistent sizes and missing doors.
* Someone had a spider that moved fine on the floor but started breaking when transitioning to walls/ceilings. They had to step through the gait one leg at a time to figure out what was wrong.
* AI kept producing a bad chopping animation, so instead of wasting more tokens prompting it, the solution was using existing mocap animations and retargeting them.
* A 3D generator ignored its own constraints, giving 5000 faces instead of 3000 and models facing the wrong direction, so you need actual validation instead of trusting the output.

that's the kind of stuff i wanted to turn into reusable workflows, including what to try when the obvious approach doesn't work.

maybe the MCP's built-in skills already handle some of this, fair enough. i'm not claiming mine are better without benchmarks. just trying to make something useful for people who keep running into these issues.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body: /shrug, you do you.  I've just run into all of those and going "hey, this shouldn't happen, let's update Claude.md with instructions not to do this" has been enough so far.  Skills tend to be token devouring monsters that often just clearer prompt instructions can solve for.

comments.author: Fine-Reflection-7530
comments.body:
Hey guys, I’ve seen a lot of comments, so I just want to clarify a few things.

First of all, yes, this project was made with AI. I’m not hiding that. But the knowledge behind it comes from real game developers’ experiences. I went through videos of people making games with AI, the problems they ran into, and the ways they figured out how to solve them. The goal was to turn those lessons into reusable skills that AI agents can actually follow.

I made ForgeSkills for people who struggle with AI-assisted game development and end up wasting thousands of tokens trying to fix something that should be relatively simple. The idea is to give AI agents better workflows for debugging, 3D modeling, animation, VFX, and matching visual references instead of having them repeatedly guess and fail.

I’ve also seen the hate comments, and honestly, some of them make it sound like I’m trying to sell some bullshit product. I’m not. It’s open source, and I’m sharing it for free.

You don’t have to like the project, and I’m completely open to genuine criticism or suggestions on how to improve it. But at the end of the day, I’m trying to contribute something useful to the community. Even if it only helps a few people, I think that’s worth doing.

That’s it. If you see something wrong with the project, tell me what it is and I’ll try to improve it. That’s the whole point.
